title: Moab's Downfall
english: And Israel was inaccessible, and thus they were exceedingly bitter and malicious in disposition, withdrawing their support and persuading others to attack against the God over all.

This attitude persisted until the end, and even when Israel suffered misfortunes brought upon itself by God, they rejoiced and gloated over them, those who accused God of being utterly unable to do anything, the God who promised to save those who worship him.
The prophet Jeremiah bears witness to this in his vision against them, declaring that their strength is shattered and they will be made drunk for exalting themselves against the Lord.
Jeremiah says, 'The horn of Moab is broken, and its strength is shattered. Make him drunk, for he has exalted himself against the Lord.' (Jeremiah 48:2-3)
Furthermore, Jeremiah says that Arioth is taken and the fortresses are seized, and Moab will perish from among the people because they have exalted themselves against the Lord. (Jeremiah 48:24)
For indeed at intervals the tyrant of 70,400 Assyrians and Babylonians came, devastating Judah and capturing the cities of Samaria.
Meanwhile, the Moabites, mocking the destroyed nation, celebrated immoderately and reproached, while they were scattering the glory of God.
Thus they too are given over to desolation, utterly destroyed together with their cities, people, and every house, to the point where it seems they may not even exist.
The vision mentioned earlier remembers these events that have happened to them, clearly demonstrating wrath from above, and says, 'At night the Moabite perishes.' (Jeremiah 48:20)
For the wall of the Moabite territory was destroyed by night.

According to some investigators, when the Babylonians were about to wage war against the Moabites, an earthquake occurred, devastating the metropolis and causing its wall to collapse by itself in the night and darkness, before the enemies even approached, and the Moabites' hope of salvation perished.

The Moabites had become terrible and uncultured, and having emboldened themselves by the deceits of demons, and by means of magical art seeking to increase themselves against the whole hand, and even of Israel itself, if God should defend it.
Therefore, in the so-called Lebedon, their altar was and a sanctuary not insignificant, which place they had come to build.
There they performed divinations, thought greatly, and held the place most sacred above all others.
But it is said that Lebedon, where the Moabites' altar is, will be destroyed, and the workshop of their divination will be destroyed.

The prophet warns the Moabites, saying, 'But lament, for yourselves'; for they had often raised their eyebrows high, delighting in the misfortunes of others, but now the war runs against them themselves, and the damage from here onward hangs upon the heads of their impieties. (Jeremiah 48:31)
The Moabites are told to lament for themselves, for they had often raised their eyebrows high, delighting in the misfortunes of others.
There they will ascend…
translator_notes: The Greek text begins mid-sentence with 'ς καὶ δυσάντητος ἦν ὁ Ἰσραὴλ', suggesting a preceding word like 'καὶ' or 'δὲ' is missing; the initial 'ς' is treated as a terminal sigma from a prior word, not translated.
Numerical notation '70.400' is rendered as '70,400' in English for readability, preserving the value as given.
The text contains multiple instances of isolated digits (e.g., '6' and '9'); these are interpreted as editorial markers or folio numbers, not part of the narrative, and are omitted.
The final fragment 'Ἐκεῖ ἀναβήσεσθ' is translated literally as 'There they will ascend…' due to its incomplete nature.

title: Futility of Idolatry
english: I am declaring your sufferings and making known the calamity that has befallen you.
For the prophet said at the beginning of the vision, 'Moab will be destroyed at night', and 'the wall of Moab will be destroyed at night'. (Isaiah 15:1)

When an earthquake occurred, the wall of Moab was destroyed, and it was what the Moabites had rebuilt, and before the enemies' attack it was almost shaken from its foundations and fell, and thus they spent their labor in vain.
The Assyrians and Babylonians took the entire land without difficulty.
My inner parts will resound over your calamities like a well-tuned lyre, and I will make your suffering heard; just as your wall, which you rebuilt, was destroyed, but not for any useful purpose.
For when the wall fell automatically, none of the things that happened in all of Moab, or in other cities and lands, were hidden.
And it will be that when you are ashamed, Moab will labor in vain on the altars, and will enter the handmade things, so as to pray, but will not be able to save itself.

Furthermore, the same thing will happen to you again, which will be a shame and a disgrace to you; for you will labor in vain, filling the altars with blood, and making the sacrifices endless, and offering prayers to the handmade things, but they will not be able to deliver you from the evils that have been imposed.
For what power is in idols, lifeless things, which are also human discoveries, and have as their creators those who worship them?
Therefore, as the blessed David says, let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.

The Moabites had become extremely superstitious, engaging in bird augury, false prophecy, and the telling of portents, and had greatly dared to trust in the evils of magic, thinking that these practices would give them an advantage against their enemies, but they had erred in their hope, calling upon lifeless matter for assistance through sacrifices and prayer.
This is the word that the Lord spoke concerning Moab, when he also spoke.

This is the vision that was spoken concerning the Moabites by God, when he also spoke, that is, even if before the words came through me, and most of what he had spoken about it, and upon myriads it itself…
translator_notes: The phrase 'upon myriads it itself' is unclear and may be a corruption in the text.
The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the beginning or end.
The text ends mid-sentence with 'ἐπὶ μυρίοις αὐτὴ'.
The Greek phrase 'ἐπὶ μυρίοις αὐτὴ' appears at the end of the text and is rendered literally as 'upon myriads it itself…' with a trailing ellipsis to indicate the fragmentary nature.

title: God's Protection of His People
english: The nations are clearly visible, and their multitude is named as they rush upon the regions, or the cities of Judaea, with a powerful and violent force, making noises and causing disturbances, much like a large body of water or a force carried with great momentum, but not like the sea, which overwhelms those who oppose it.
God calls their back a multitude of nations, because many nations are pursued by them, and the pursuers run after the backs of those who flee, doing so in every way and with great persistence.

What happens next is that God will send them backward, pursuing them from afar, much like chaff blown away by the wind, or like dust raised by a chariot, for what is easily blown away, like dust from a wheel or a threshing floor, by a violent wind, is indeed a pitiful sight.

Sennacherim, a fugitive, departed, and the God of all spoke to him through the voice of Isaiah, saying, 'I will put a bridle in your mouth, and a bit in your lips, and I will turn you back on the way you came' (Isaiah 30:28).
In the evening, there will be mourning, but it will not be before morning, that is, the weeping will cease and come to an end.
Earlier, it was said that Rhapsakes, having encircled Jerusalem with his army, and not having taken it far, having threatened, perished with his whole army before dawn and day.
Mourning, therefore, will be in the evening, certainly, because those in Jerusalem expected to be attacked in the morning, but the war's attack ceased before dawn.
Through this, God says that there will be mourning in the evening, but it will not last until morning, and the weeping will cease and come to an end.
As fear will drive out those who suffer, God will help, surprisingly destroying the enemy's phalanxes and driving out their leader from Judea's land.
The blessed David explains this, saying that 'in the evening we will weep, but in the morning, we will experience joy' (Psalm 30:5).
This is the lot of those who have plundered and ravaged God's people, treating them as their own inheritance.

God reproaches the Israelites because they have done what would have been expected to completely destroy the nation, but instead, he pities it again and punishes with death those who ravage the people entrusted to him.

For when the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered Adam's sons, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of God's angels, and the Lord's portion was his people, Jacob, the measuring line of his inheritance, Israel (Deuteronomy 32:8-9).
translator_notes: The translation aims to preserve the original word order and meaning, while also conveying the author's voice and literary style.
